newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak president urges prosecutor's dismissal.
newsitem.headline: Slovak president urges prosecutor's dismissal.

text.p: Slovakia's president on Thursday accused the country's chief prosecutor of showing "professional and moral incompetence" in failing to pursue key criminal cases and urged parliament to dismiss him.

President Michal Kovac gave a news conference a list of 26 unsolved cases, including the kidnapping of his own son, Michal Kovac Junior, and what he said were illegal deals in privatising state property.
But Prosecutor General Michal Valo later gave his own news conference and rejected the allegations, saying he had no plans to bow to pressure from the president to resign.
"He has neither the legal nor moral right to call for my resignation," said Valo, who was appointed by Kovac in 1994 but can only be dismissed by parliament.
Kovac said: "By his unwillingness to pursue these criminal cases to the end...(Valo) has shown professional and moral incompetence."
"I appeal to parliament, all deputies, the minister of interior .. all parliamentary parties to redress this bad situation," he said.
Michal Kovac Junior was abducted in 1995, bundled into the boot of his car and dumped outside a police station in Austria, where he had been sought on suspicion of fraud.
Kovac has attributed the kidnapping to a political vendetta between himself and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar and accused the secret service (SIS) of organising the kidnap.
Two state detectives were sacked after their investigations led them to suspect SIS involvement. A third investigator adjourned the case last May due to lack of evidence.
"Who is responsible for failing to ensure the SIS...should provide information which would clear suspicion of the involvement of SIS officers and equipment," Kovac asked.
At his news conference following the president's, Valo rejected the allegations, saying they were based on unofficial sources, press reports and incorrect data.
"By his allegations the president has undermined the confidence of the population in the police, the judiciary and the prosecutor's office," Valo said.
Kovac deplored the state of justice in Slovakia, saying it was subjected more to politics than to law.
"My efforts to point out the need to preserve the functioning of the legal system of our state is not an attempt to criminalise the political and economic environment, but to cleanse it," Kovac said.
